blocks.text: A laser therapy device delivers concentrated light energy to tissue for a specific therapeutic or surgical purpose. Depending on the laser type, it may be used for tissue cutting, coagulation, ablation, dermatological procedures, ophthalmic treatment or selected physiotherapy applications.
For an OSCE, the key is to identify the device's intended use, explain the basic principle, demonstrate laser safety, and recognise the risks of eye injury, burns and fire.

Important: “Laser therapy device” is a broad category. A low-level laser used in physiotherapy is very different from a high-power surgical CO₂ or Nd:YAG laser. Their indications, settings, hazards and precautions are not interchangeable.
Name: Medical laser therapy device.
Classification: Therapeutic or surgical medical equipment, depending on the application.
Principle: Stimulated emission produces light that can be delivered in a controlled beam.
Main function: Delivers optical energy to selected tissue to produce a defined biological effect.
Distinguishing features: A control console or power unit, a laser source, a delivery system such as a handpiece or fibre, controls and safety features.
Used in selected rehabilitation and pain-management settings. It is intended to produce photobiomodulatory effects rather than deliberately cut or ablate tissue.
Commonly used for precise tissue cutting, vaporisation and ablation in selected surgical procedures.
Depending on wavelength and system design, these may be used for coagulation, selected ophthalmic procedures, dermatology and other specialised applications.

rows: Surgery
Cutting, vaporisation or coagulation of selected tissues
Dermatology
Treatment of selected vascular lesions, pigmentation, scars or hair reduction, depending on the laser
Ophthalmology
Specific retinal or anterior-segment procedures using appropriate laser systems
Physiotherapy
Selected musculoskeletal applications using photobiomodulation devices
Dentistry
Selected soft-tissue or other dental procedures, depending on the laser
Urology and other specialties
Certain endoscopic or tissue procedures using specialty-specific systems

blocks.text: OSCE point: Never state that every laser treats all these conditions. The wavelength, power, pulse characteristics, delivery system and approved clinical indication determine what the device can safely do.
Allows authorised users to select and verify the permitted operating mode and parameters, such as power, pulse duration and exposure time.
A handpiece, optical fibre, articulated arm or other system directs the laser energy to the treatment site.
A trigger, foot pedal or equivalent control activates the laser according to the device design.
May include an emergency stop, key switch, standby mode, warning indicator and interlock system.
Wavelength- and optical-density-rated eyewear protects the eyes of staff and patients when required by the laser safety protocol.
Other components may include cooling systems, aiming beams, smoke evacuation, fibre connectors and cooling accessories, depending on the model.
Can deliver energy precisely to a selected tissue.
Some procedures produce less bleeding because certain lasers coagulate vessels while treating tissue.
May reduce the need for conventional incisions in selected procedures.
Allows controlled treatment of specific tissue depths when the correct system and technique are used.
Some devices are portable and non-invasive, particularly certain low-level laser systems.
Can be useful in specialised procedures where conventional instruments are less suitable.
Equipment may be expensive and requires specialised training.
Incorrect settings or technique can cause burns, scarring or unintended tissue damage.
Direct or reflected beams can injure the eyes.
High-power surgical lasers can ignite combustible materials.
Laser plume from tissue procedures may contain harmful particles and requires appropriate control.
Treatment effectiveness varies by indication; evidence for some low-level laser applications remains mixed.
Not every laser is suitable for every skin type, tissue or clinical condition.
Before treatment:
Confirm the patient's identity, diagnosis, treatment site and intended procedure.
Explain the procedure, expected effects, risks and alternatives; obtain informed consent.
Verify the device type, wavelength, intended use and required accessories.
Check the device, delivery system, safety controls and maintenance status.
Ensure the operator is trained and authorised to use the equipment.
Apply the required laser safety precautions, including a controlled treatment area and warning signage.
Provide wavelength-appropriate protective eyewear to the patient and everyone present, as required by the safety protocol.
Remove or protect combustible materials and follow fire-safety procedures.
For surgical procedures, use appropriate plume evacuation and other specialty-specific protective measures.
Inspect the treatment area and confirm the correct settings against the prescribed protocol.

Laser safety is wavelength-specific. Ordinary sunglasses are not an acceptable substitute for certified laser protective eyewear. The eyewear must match the laser's wavelength and required optical density.

items: Correct patient, indication and treatment site
Controlled area and warning signs in place
Fire precautions and plume controls addressed where applicable

blocks.text: The exact operating sequence varies substantially by device. In an OSCE, describe the general safety sequence and follow the manufacturer's instructions rather than inventing settings.
Confirm the diagnosis, treatment site, contraindications and prescribed treatment plan.
Control access to the treatment area, display the required warning signs, provide suitable eyewear and address fire and plume risks.

items: Step 3 — Inspect and configure the device

blocks.text: Check the power unit, delivery system and safety features. Select only the prescribed, device-appropriate parameters.

items: Step 4 — Prepare the patient and treatment site

blocks.text: Position the patient, expose the intended site and prepare the skin or tissue according to the procedure. Apply any required protective measures.
Activate the laser only when ready, using the approved technique and prescribed parameters. Observe the treatment site and patient response continuously.

items: Step 6 — Stop and secure the equipment

blocks.text: Return the device to standby, deactivate it and secure it according to the manufacturer's instructions. Do not leave an armed laser unattended.
Assess the treatment site and patient response, provide aftercare instructions, document the device and parameters used, and report any adverse event.

content_groups.group_title: Key parameters an examiner may ask about

blocks.text: Wavelength: Influences tissue absorption and penetration.
Power: Rate of energy delivery, usually expressed in watts.
Energy: Total energy delivered, expressed in joules.
Power density (irradiance): Power delivered per unit area.
Exposure time: Duration of delivery.
Pulse characteristics: Continuous or pulsed delivery, depending on the device.
For some applications, fluence (energy per unit area) is also important. The correct combination depends on the laser, tissue and clinical indication.
There is no single universal contraindication list for every medical laser. The decision depends on the device, treatment target and patient.

rows: Direct or reflected exposure to eyes
Can cause serious ocular injury; use wavelength-specific protection
Pregnancy
Assess the specific procedure, treatment site and device; do not assume all laser procedures have identical risks
Photosensitivity or photosensitising medication
Relevant to some treatments; assess the specific laser and indication
Suspicious or undiagnosed skin lesion
Obtain appropriate diagnostic assessment before cosmetic treatment or ablation
Active infection or impaired wound healing
May require deferral or a modified treatment plan
Combustible materials and oxygen-rich environments
Particularly important with high-power surgical lasers
Implanted devices or nearby sensitive structures
Follow device-specific and specialty-specific guidance

blocks.text: Thermal burns and blistering.
Pain, swelling or erythema.
Pigmentary changes and scarring.
Ocular injury.
Infection or delayed healing.
Unintended tissue damage.
Fire or ignition during certain procedures.
Inhalation exposure to surgical plume when it is not adequately controlled.
If a laser-related eye injury, burn or fire occurs, stop treatment, secure the equipment if safe to do so, initiate appropriate emergency procedures and arrange urgent assessment as indicated.
There is no universal “normal laser result”; findings depend on the treatment being performed.

rows: Low-level laser therapy
Often no visible immediate tissue change
Unexpected pain, burning or skin injury
Dermatological laser
Device- and treatment-specific redness or swelling may occur
Excessive blistering, severe pain, unexpected whitening or darkening, or extensive burns
Surgical laser
Intended cutting, vaporisation or coagulation
Uncontrolled bleeding, unintended tissue injury or fire
Ophthalmic laser
Intended therapeutic effect assessed by the treating specialist
New visual disturbance, significant pain or other unexpected symptoms

blocks.text: Do not judge effectiveness solely by the immediate appearance of the treatment site. Some effects require follow-up assessment.
Confirm the indication and use a device suitable for the child's age and clinical needs.
Explain the procedure in age-appropriate language and obtain appropriate consent and assent.
Ensure correctly fitting protective eyewear and supervision.
Consider movement, anxiety and whether additional support or specialist care is needed.
Use paediatric-specific protocols and settings where applicable.
For surgical procedures, carefully assess airway, oxygen and fire risks.
Avoid cosmetic or therapeutic laser treatment without an appropriate clinical indication and specialist assessment.

subsections.subsection_title: Common OSCE questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. Identify this instrument.
This is a medical laser therapy device. It delivers concentrated optical energy for a specified therapeutic or surgical application.
Q2. What is the basic principle of a laser?
LASER stands for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. The device produces light with specific optical properties that can be delivered to tissue to achieve a defined effect.
Q3. Mention four medical applications of lasers.
Selected surgical procedures, dermatological treatments, ophthalmic procedures and certain physiotherapy applications.
Q4. What are the main components?
The control console, laser source, delivery system, activation controls and safety features. Protective eyewear and other accessories are also required as appropriate.
Q5. What is the most important safety precaution?
Preventing hazardous eye exposure by controlling the treatment area and using certified protective eyewear appropriate to the laser's wavelength and required optical density.
Q6. Why is smoke evacuation necessary during some laser procedures?
Laser treatment of tissue can generate a plume containing particles and potentially harmful substances. Appropriate local exhaust ventilation or smoke evacuation reduces exposure.
Q7. What is the difference between low-level laser therapy and a surgical laser?

Low-level laser or photobiomodulation devices are intended to produce biological effects without deliberately ablating tissue. Surgical lasers deliver energy for effects such as cutting, vaporisation or coagulation. Their power, parameters, safety requirements and indications differ.
Q8. Name four complications of medical laser use.
Burns, scarring, ocular injury and unintended tissue damage. Depending on the procedure, fire, infection and plume exposure are also important risks.
Avoid these errors:
Assuming all medical lasers work in the same way.
Giving treatment settings without knowing the specific device or indication.
Using ordinary sunglasses instead of wavelength-appropriate protective eyewear.
Forgetting to mention controlled access and warning signs.
Ignoring the risks of fire and surgical plume.
Assuming that absence of immediate redness means treatment has failed.
Claiming that laser therapy is effective for every pain or skin condition.
Forgetting to check the emergency stop and return the device to standby after use.

Examiner tip: If the station shows a particular laser, identify its intended application before discussing indications, settings or complications. A physiotherapy laser and a high-power surgical laser should not be described as interchangeable instruments.
1. What determines the appropriate protective eyewear for a medical laser?

items: The colour of the laser housing
The laser wavelength and required optical density

blocks.text: 2. Which is a major hazard of some high-power surgical lasers?

items: Reduced blood pressure in every patient

blocks.text: 3. What is the main distinction between low-level laser therapy and a surgical laser?

items: They are identical devices with different names

blocks.text: Low-level devices aim for photobiomodulation; surgical lasers may cut, ablate or coagulate tissue

items: Surgical lasers never require eye protection

blocks.text: Instrument: Medical laser therapy device.
Principle: Delivers controlled optical energy to tissue.
Uses: Selected surgical, dermatological, ophthalmic and physiotherapy applications.
Main components: Console, laser source, delivery system, activation controls and safety features.
Major hazards: Eye injury, burns, fire and surgical plume.
Essential safety rule: Use wavelength-appropriate protective eyewear and follow the device-specific safety protocol.
